lesson.heading: Name the parts before you listen
lesson.text: Diagram completion asks you to label a machine or a device. Look at the picture first and give every part a name in your head. If you cannot name it, describe what it probably does - that is often the word you will hear.

examples.note: *The water passes through the pipe and ...*
*There is a wheel on the side, which is attached to ...*
*The water in the pool was becoming quite polluted so a pump ...*
*A small spring in the centre causes the toy ...*
*At the bottom of the system there is a storage tank ...*
*There is a very fine grille at different points ...*

lesson.heading: The verbs of machines
lesson.text: Descriptions of how something works use verbs you rarely need in conversation. Learning a handful of them turns a confusing extract into a clear one.
lesson.note: In the Party Popper task the verbs actually heard were *turn, pop, hold, wind, generate, wrap, pull, explode, push, rotate, activate*.

lesson.heading: Instruments and their purpose
lesson.note: *It is used to + verb* is the standard pattern for defining a device. Expect it in Sections 2 and 4.

lesson.heading: Movement is in the preposition

right.label: How it moves
examples: The paper was then wrapped **around** the ...

lesson.note: The preposition is often the whole answer. Miss it and you have the right object in the wrong place.

lesson.heading: A process runs on sequencers
lesson.text: When someone describes a process, the stages are held together by sequencing words. They tell you a new step - and usually a new answer - is starting.

examples.text: **First,** gather together all of the things you need.
**Then,** *place* your present on the opened wrapping paper and *cut* a suitable amount using the scissors.
**Next,** *wrap* the paper around the present and *stick* it down with sticky tape.
**Then, neatly** *fold* up each of the ends of the paper and *stick* them down.

lesson.text: In a diagram task, some parts are never labelled. If a name in the option list is never mentioned, that is normal - check *why* the speaker ruled it out rather than forcing it into a gap.

exercises.prompt: Match each instrument with what it is used to do.
*It then passes ___ a pipe and into the tank.*
exercises.hint: (in one side and out the other)
exercises.explanation: *Through* means entering and leaving. *Along* would mean following the outside of the pipe.

exercises.prompt: Put the stages of wrapping a present in order.
exercises.answer: First, gather everything; next, wrap the paper; finally, tie the ribbon.
exercises.explanation: *First*, *next* and *finally* mark the beginning, the middle and the end of a process.

exercises.prompt: You hear *A small spring in the centre causes the toy to ...* Which part is being described?
options: a coil of metal that pushes back when pressed
exercises.explanation: A spring is a coil. Picturing the object is what lets you recognise the word when it arrives.

exercises.prompt: Sort these verbs by what they describe.

exercises.statement: In a diagram-labelling task with six options and four gaps, every option is used once.
exercises.explanation: Two options are left over. In the Party Popper task the cooling fan and the winder were both ruled out by what the speaker said.

exercises.prompt: *This then forces the air ___.* Which word describes air being pushed up out of the machine?
exercises.explanation: *Upwards* gives the direction. Prepositions and adverbs of movement are often the answer itself.

exercises.prompt: *At the bottom of the system there is a storage ___ that holds the water.*
exercises.explanation: *At the bottom of the system* tells you where to look on the diagram before the word even arrives.

exercises.statement: *It is used to measure temperature* is a standard way of defining what a device does.
exercises.explanation: *Be used to + verb* is the usual pattern. Recognising it tells you a definition is coming.

exercises.prompt: Why is it worth naming every part of a diagram before the recording begins?
options: Because the names are always the answers
Because you are marked on the labels you predict
Because you will recognise the word far faster when you hear it
Because the speaker reads out the diagram in order
exercises.explanation: Prediction buys you speed. With one listening only, recognition has to be instant.
